newsitem.title: ITALY: FEATURE - Cellulite not only problem for celluloid girls.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Cellulite not only problem for celluloid girls.

text.p: The path to a career as a top women's fashion model is littered with tales of what might have been.
Many aspirants tower over other women, weigh about 55 kg (125 pounds), still look great on only four hours' sleep and can dazzle the camera time and again under intense pressure.
They can also survive in heavy winter clothes under baking lights and swing their hips rhythmically along a catwalk in an impossibly narrow skirt atop shoes with 10 cm (four inch) heels.
But they are still only about halfway there.
Backstage during Milan fashion week willowy models in their teens and 20s earnestly compared notes on the tools of their trade -- diet, make-up, hair and most of all patience.
The dressing room behind a catwalk is a babble of languages as women from many lands compare translucent complexions, tease strands of long wispy hair or make microscopic adjustments to make-up.

Blonde Czech supermodel Eva Herzigova, 24, reckons it takes 90 minutes to get set for the runway, with hair, make-up and clothing in place. "It depends on how difficult the make-up is and how much they have to do," she told Reuters.
During Milan's week of autumn/winter 1997/98 collections, models tore from show to show, often hurtling right across town.
Herzigova, backstage for Les Copains show, said on one day she had made five appearances, changing make-up five times, but her skin somehow survived with no ill effects.

Rushing between shows is easier for some than for others. Celebrities like Herzigova ride in chauffeur-driven cars but one aspiring model remembered a hair-raising race through traffic-choked Milan straddling the pillion of a moped.
MODELLING MYTHS
Food and fashion week don't mix as the slender models, many of them nearly 180 cm (six feet) tall, say they get scant time to eat between shoots and walks.
Some must make an effort to keep their weight up, few said they actively dieted and one famous model was once spotted munching a takeaway hamburger backstage.
Herzigova, her long slim legs clad in black slacks, said she just tried to eat healthily. "I love Italian food. I hate chocolate and I hate sweets, so they're not appealing to me."
Presentation is everything in fashion but women have little time to change in the course of a show.
Anyone with a seat near the start of the catwalk can see that slow, sexy saunter turn into an undignified gallop the instant the girl thinks she is out of sight.
Viviana, 23, a law student who declined to give her surname, helps models change during shows. She said swapping an entire outfit takes one to two minutes -- if nothing goes wrong.
"I remember once a thin leather shoe strap came off in my hand. The designer was standing right behind me and in the end I just knotted it and hoped he didn't notice," she said.
Classic accidents are laddered tights and broken zippers -- and then the best remedy is the good old-fashioned safety pin.
SHOWBIZ JUNGLE
Modelling can be lonely, especially for teenagers flying off to shoot on locations around the world.
"I haven't seen my family for three months. I'm going to be 19 soon and it's the longest I've ever been away from home," said one dark-haired girl from the Middle East.
"Models just bond together because they understand the pressures and stress of work and travel," said a fair-haired 17-year-old from Boston, who declined to give her name.
Her boyfriend, himself a model, lives in Paris. "We understand each others' work pressures," she said.
Despite the cameraderie, it's also a cut-throat world.
"I've had other models tell me to go the wrong way for a casting. There's lots of competition," the 17-year-old said.
Pay is a sensitive topic. Magazine reports say Herzigova earns nearly half a million dollars a year although she herself declined to comment.
A magazine shoot in Milan brings a model agency about 500,000 lire ($295) per day, although the model herself will probably see about half of that.
"And catalogues are not good but you have to do those to pay the rent," one commented wryly.

No one would admit in front of others how much she earned. One said she once upset a fellow model by revealing how much she was paid for a job. "This business of how much you're paid has a lot to do with keeping your self-esteem in the face of so much competition," she added.
Backstage, however, the atmosphere is friendly, with groups of models sitting crosslegged on the floor and chatting as they while away the minutes until the show gets going.
Some read books but American Sibyl Buck, 23, was calmly struggling through her first attempt to knit a sweater. "I can do it while I'm waiting for fittings or right before the shows," Buck said.
"It's so therapeutic because I have to concentrate to make sure I don't drop stitches...it takes my mind off anything that's bothering me." ($ = 1691 Italian Lire)
